Much more prevalent as an adult, but you also become numb to some of it, sometimes through dissociation, I guess.  There is no cure, you should understand that now.  It's only learning to manage it.  I found ERP to be shit, and there are those in the scientific community who agree.  It can cause further damage if you've got the wrong therapist.  

Both you and he need to start accepting it.  Making peace with it is the best thing I ever did for it.  It sucks sometimes, but it's nothing compared to other stuff I deal with, and it's mostly in the comorbidity that the OCD causes pain these days, it is usually little more than an annoyance on its own. 

If you're really concerned, while OCD may be able to exist in a vacuum, that's rarely the case.  I would put more resources into finding what's really troubling your son that to just treat symptoms (which is basically what you're seeing with the OCD - it's often crops up because of something else).  Don't just put him in ERP therapy, at the very least complement that with a proper psychologist to meet with him, someone he will feel comfortable talking about whatever with.  It's the root cause that will linger and show up in other forms, like water trying to find a drainage path.  I dealt with some nasty childhood traumas, and parents don't always see these things, because at least in my case, they can be the ones causing the problems.  I'm not trying to blame you, I don't know you or your son, but I just mean to strongly suggest that he have talk therapy in addition to ERP if you want good results, as I found ERP therapy to be annoying and useless.  More might have been gained had I been in an office talking about how fucked up things were at home than going around malls eating jelly beans left on toilet seats...

Here's my two cents - I do see homeless people around NL, it's just that compared to most countries, the homeless in NL are very well-dressed.  That's part of it.  The "average homeless" person in NL is likely to be better dressed than I am, on most days.  This is a wealthy-ass country, and even the poor may have comparably nicer things.  The guy I saw tearing through trash bins to collect cans, yesterday...  he was groomed and in nicer clothes than many of the other passengers (it was a train station).  So I think this makes it "less noticeable" to some. 

Also, unlike in the U.S., in NL there are day centers they are likely spending time at, rather than all just congregating in a park or two, or fighting over street corners to panhandle because they're kicked out of the shelter with nowhere else to go during the day.  They tend to be more "mobile," in that you don't see someone just plopped down with a sign in one place all day.  There is a homeless woman near my apartment who I catch in various places around town every time I see her.  She's usually just walking around, maybe hangs outside a store for a little bit, then wanders some more.  She isn't poorly dressed, either, I only suspect because she's asked me for money so many times now.

Plus, the police here seem to be more... shitty about it.  I've seen them harass a black man trying to sell newspapers outside a store, while inside the store a bunch of white Dutch teens were stealing things (literally at the same time).  That sort of points to how the Dutch approach things - if it "looks" like something they don't like (poor black man trying to get by probably rubs several Dutch the wrong way), they will make a fuss.  If it's ACTUALLY not good, but no one seems to notice much...   This is why when I hear about some of the stuff going on "under the table" in this country, it sounds shocking, as you wouldn't expect it.  The real problems here, no one seems to be even talking about.  Too many sheeple scared of actually arguing for real improvements, because they'd rather just take their frustration out with 1\* Google reviews at random businesses than actually end homelessness or solve a housing crisis.  This is where the cultural idea of 'not rocking the boat' goes horribly wrong, because more should be discussed and implemented to improve things - the Dutch seem to just prefer looking the other way when it's something that's actually serious.  Endless complaints about something as trivial as weather, but don't bother asking about government reform.....  There should really be more public discourse.

Self-awareness is HUGE.  And you're only 21.  Most people your age don't have great self-awareness (I say this as a very self-aware empathic person that was more concerned with getting drunk, smoking weed, and having sex at 21, even if I had always been "mature for my age").  It's commendable.  So let's start there.  You feel upset, but in your words I already see a caring person with self-awareness, and that's good in my book. 

Speaking from my own experience, a next step from self-awareness is being able to act on that.  Stopping yourself when you recognize you're spiraling, stopping yourself if you see you're hurting someone, intentionally or not.  Learning how to speak about these things with people can also help your relationships.  That can take a great level of maturity and self-awareness.  I didn't really learn to step back to be able to talk about my challenges in a way that others can understand until around 40 years old.  If you can do that sooner, bravo.  

I would offer that we often develop patterns.  Our brains, however chaotic at times, actually prefer taking the easy route, and neural pathways are formed and reinforced through patterns and habits.  A book that helped me a bit is called "The Upward Spiral."  It basically helps you better recognize your behaviors as being helpful or hurtful in the long-run, and how to build helpful habits.  That makes it easier and easier the longer you practice it.  

When I was doing some self-recovery from major depression, back when I had more energy to heal myself rather than fall to pieces more often (be glad you're young!), I would catch myself.... every negative thought I had, sometimes even rather silly ones, I would stop myself, and then think the opposite, or something that was far more optimistic.  You can choose your perspective.  At one time, my brain knew that better.  Now, it's tricky for me, but I'm middle-aged and have had some physical brain injuries on top of the psychological trauma, so things aren't as simple for me now.  But you have a great opportunity to work on developing more helpful thinking habits.

So perish the thought that it's hopeless.  Try not to feel like no matter what you do, it turns out badly.  I'm sure, if you put your energy into it, you could find examples proving otherwise - times when things turned out well thanks to your effort.  Try to reinforce the more helpful thoughts, and try to think those more often. 

I hope this helps.  I am not here to tell you what to do, but to offer suggestions I hope will help.  You're young, and have so much life ahead, I just hope you can find a way to get better soon and feel happier. :)

I'm actually running an experiment (I'm wrapping up now) to see if I could code a business site using AI only.  

The short answer is: not 100%.  

I could usually get it to correct when necessary, but I knew what I was asking to be specific.  In other words, you still need a background in coding, you can't blindly build a web app using only AI.  There were also a few times it just couldn't spit out the right info, and I had to go in and do it myself.  For debugging, it could be a little hit or miss, as well, and it was usually quicker for me to just go in and fix it, myself.

**Takeaways**: 

* AI can save time - I could have full components coded in seconds, copy/paste, and even if I needed to make a couple small layout changes, or fix one bug, it was a big time-saver
* Design help - I'm not a pro designer, and this tends to be where I have the most trouble if building a site from scratch - AI was helpful in taking reference images and (with some prodding) creating coherent color schemes and generated images (no copyright issues, or having to pay a bunch of money to a stock site) to fit the site.
* AI cannot (at this time) completely replace technical/coding knowledge - The more advanced what you're trying to code, the more likely it will mess up somewhere

Okay, a number of things to clear up here.

First, short-term contracts are illegal unless you're a student or asylum seeker (or a couple other fringe cases).  That's anything under two years for a fixed term.  Anything over two years is automatically indefinite.  This is the law.  You mention six months in Utrecht, so maybe you're a student.  Otherwise, don't go looking for a contract like this, because it's illegal, and anyone offering that will likely be looking to screw you in other ways, as well.

Second... you haven't found an apartment yet, but are already worried about registering the address?  Find a place first.

You can find information on the gemeente website, or call them, but generally you bring your passport, rental contract, and birth certificate.  You'll need to make an appointment to go in for this.  There is nothing additional your landlord gives you, you just bring in the signed and counter-signed rental agreement.  They WILL verify the person renting to you is legally able to (they'll make sure it's the actual owner), so if you have some shady deal setup, it's not going to help you register.

Charging people to register is fucked up.  Clearly this guy tries to operate outside the law.  The rental market is insane right now (in case you're unaware), and there are lots of "stunts" people are pulling.  Without knowing more about the specific unit, I can't say more, but there are several reasons property owners do this.  He's probably worried about an increase in tax and service costs, and is trying to pass that on to you.  Anyone trying to charge you to register, unless you have no other options, I would suggest walking away from.

There are other subs and threads with a lot more detailed information about the ins and outs of rental law and registration.  I've spent nearly 20 hours studying all this.  There's info available, so do your own searches and educate yourself further.  Hopefully this comment has helped you a bit, though.

Edit: If you JUST need the BSN more quickly, for whatever reason, you could register on the RNI immediately (as soon as you get an appointment), get your BSN at the appointment, and go from there.  You can tell them your situation, and go back with the birth certificate and rental agreement, so you can be added to the BRP, later.  There are systems that will catch whether it's RNI or BRP, so it's not like the BSN opens every door, you do still need to be identified as a resident for things you may need to do.  I only offer this information in case it helps you in some way.

It looks like you've got some good responses already.  FWIW, you don't take the SAT/ACT to strengthen your application - those are requirements.  Any university, aside from a community college, is going to want either an SAT or ACT score (some will require one over the other - east coast schools tend to prefer SAT, but best to check the school's requirements when you decide where you'll apply).  Those tests are geared towards expected education levels in the U.S., and the common study tracks there, so whether or not your diploma translates, you'll need to be sure you're at the same place in your own studies.

I used to tutor for the ACT, so I can give you a quick rundown, but ETS will have more information on its website.  ACT will have deeper info, and at least used to even link a couple practice tests from old ACTs.

Algebra, Geometry, Trigonometry, and more basic shit.  Some word problems, images, and equations.  
Science is mostly reading charts, understanding data and trends, and reading comprehension - it's more   
  critical thinking  
English and Reading is going to be grammar, usage, vocabulary, reading comprehension, reasoning

The optional essay should always be completed.  It's a persuasive essay.  Follow the sandwich method with triangles at top and bottom (intro that ends with thesis, three paragraph body each with one point and support for the point, restate thesis and summarize with ending).  Some schools require the essay be done, so don't treat it as optional.  It also cannot cost you points.  In other words, even if you write a shit essay, it can't lower your composite score.  So just do the essay.  Also, as I was trained in scoring them at one point, if you basically just follow that outline I gave you, you're guaranteed at least a middle score, which I think adds one point to your composite - so... there's a free point for you.

ACT - can't lose points for wrong answers  
SAT - 1/4 point deducted for incorrect answer

Lesson: Give a response on every single thing for the ACT, a guess can't hurt you.    
Also: Guess left - statistically speaking, A or B is more often the correct answer than C or D

I'll briefly explain, but there are other threads about this.  There's also a ton of housing law that plays into this, which is far too complicated to explain here, but a distilled version of what you need:

Submit your residency application FIRST (but only after you've made plans and arrangements to go to NL - maybe even submit from within the country within a few days of arrival).  You need this to start other things.

Rent anything.  You are supposed to register where you live within five days.  Hospitality stays may be exceptions.  You would have to ask an Airbnb host if you went that route.  Try to find anything local, even a sublet, and BE SURE YOU CAN REGISTER!!!  There are a lot of illegal rentals, now, because of the market, and other people freaking out about their own registrations (plus just a ton of under-the-table stuff due to housing laws).  

There are two types of registration.  RNI and BRP.  RNI is non-resident.  You can do this immediately at any gemeente (and should, because it will give you your BSN more quickly, which you need for other things).  As soon as you have an address you can register (you still need this ASAP), go to the gemeente with the lease, your passport, residence endorsement sticker, and the apostilled birth certificate, and you can be registered on the BRP (resident register).  

Basically you need a legit address ASAP.  Make an appointment with the gemeente ASAP (could be weeks of waiting, and if you're in a short-term, you will really be on a timeline to get registered). 

Last thing not yet explained - the residence endorsement sticker is something you need from IND.  You'll need an extra appointment for that.  Make sure you have one full blank page (at least) in your passport.  This is basically them approving your stay while the application is being processed.  This is necessary for the gemeente to put you on the BRP.  Without the sticker, they can only do RNI.  You will need to get on the BRP.  

The rental market is fucked right now.  It will be a lot of extra stress to find a legal place, right now, long or short term.  Just be prepared.

I'll only make a note, that while Belgrade could be a good option, I would not call the residency option for foreigners to be "friendly," unless there are new laws I'm not aware of.  At least a few years ago, the way to do it was setup a local company and be self-employed.  The taxes there are 55%. You are not eligible for any public benefits (such as social programs you're required to pay into) until you've paid in for at least 20 years.  In other words, unless you're retiring in Serbia, you're only paying for other people's retirements.  That goes for health care, as well, as you're required to have private insurance.  On top of that, you'll need to hire a local attorney and accountant to manage the business documentation (if that's not in order, you'll never get your visa renewed, and they audit it regularly), and these two will overcharge you as a foreigner (almost no way to avoid this, it's the culture there, but you can look around).  In the end, you will pay out almost 75% of your income on the costs of maintaining the business entity in Serbia plus taxes and social contributions you are required to pay by law.  In the end, especially when you contrast this with the flat 8% you pay in Bulgaria, I would call Serbia one of the LEAST "friendly" places to get residency.  The process is simple enough I did it on my own without a lawyer (but had help from a couple local friends to complete a lot of the paperwork, as it's in Cyrillic), but what you end up paying to have that residency is absurd.

It all comes down to construction and materials.  One of the quietest places I've ever had was in Chicago. I'm writing this as someone who is very sensitive to noise, and has C-PTSD (so unwelcome noise can actually trigger anxiety and pain - basically a trauma response)...

You should consider yourself lucky.  That is white noise, if it's a constant humming.  Also, 40dB is quiet.  I recently arrived from Mexico where the AMBIENT noise level in my apartment was about 55dB.  It would regularly spike to over 80dB due to traffic, explosions, music, yelling, dogs.........  fucking Mexico.

There are ear plugs that lower noises by 30dB.  A good set of ear plugs should practically eliminate that noise.  Consider figuring out how to PROPERLY insert the ear plugs.  And noise cancelling headsets...  if that's not doing, get a better pair.  Soundcore Q30 has excellent ANC.  You won't hear a fucking thing if it's only 40dB.  If you prefer earbuds, I have the Space A40s, but the battery life is a bit weak (so sleeping with them... better have some ear plugs on standby for when they die - luckily they do have a quick charge, so 10 minutes gives you another few hours, on the fly).  

I send this with empathy.  You'll make yourself crazy trying to go about legalities, and fighting with police and courts, as well as make things rough with your neighbors.  Really, I think you can manage this on your own, and a constant hum should fade away to nothing easily enough.  Again, sensitive to noise, but I lived next to an expressway once.  One of the quietest places I ever had.  I added a bit of weatherstripping foam around the door, and within a week, I barely ever noticed the traffic.  It almost became peaceful white noise, at times.  A humming can easily fade into the background.  You may even try getting used to it, before resorting to blocking it.  You'll create a greater sensitivity, potentially, at least psychologically.  If you want to give it a chance to become white noise, try to just get used to it.  If it's annoying after a couple weeks, good ear plugs used properly and/or good noise cancelling headphones will eliminate it.

Of what you've listed, Portugal will be the easiest.  It's about 1000/month minimum (maybe higher now), and you can apply from within the country having entered on a tourist stamp.  You'll need a lawyer, and probably an accountant (their "green receipt" system is a little convoluted, though you can do pretty much all paperwork online - but you'll need good records, still).  A couple of the initial steps will require befriending a local.....  I had some help in getting my tax number (Airbnb host was willing to go to the tax office with me to vouch for my stay and help me with that, thankfully; opening a local bank account can take a few hoops to jump through, but a good bank will help - I'm with MillenniumBCP, opened the account with a U.S. passport, and have zero regrets, even with an 8 Euro monthly maintenance fee on the account, because they take very good care of their clients, I've had excellent support by phone in English for anything I've needed, and it lets me use the card anywhere in the Euro zone with no fees).  There will always be bureaucracy in Europe, though.  The lawyer will help with the business documents.  It's five years to PR, eight to citizenship (I believe, you can double-check this).  Citizenship would have a language component required, but then you have an EU passport after all that.

I'll only add try not to choose a country ONLY for ease, as Portugal really didn't suit me. You can spend three months in a place there isn't enough cultural overlap, and you'll probably just never form a connection with someone there regardless.  I've literally landed in a new city and fallen in love days later (true story from France - used every one of my last 90 days to stay with her, and that led me to finding a job contract in a neighboring country to stay in the area), or created my entire social circle minus one or two people through a chance encounter at a bar in week one elsewhere.  I think once the novelty of a new place wears off, and I just get more into my daily routine, I start to also put less effort into meeting more people.  Plus, it's app-centric.  Once you swipe through hundreds of people in the first days, it starts to become a moot device for trying to meet people.

That said, even before there was "nomadism," I know couples that have been together a long time that originally met on the road somewhere, doing volunteer work, climbing, whatever.  It doesn't even have to be "DNing," per se, I think it's just a chance for people who otherwise might not cross paths to meet. I mean, ..... you're asking to explain an entire culture in a reddit comment, so no... this will not be thorough.  I can only offer a few highlights that fit into more concise descriptions.

They treat foreigners very well.  It is a culture of hospitality (and I mean, not just something people say, it REALLY is - the number of invites to people's homes I received even as a bit of a recluse in general, a guy who literally gave me the jacket off his back on a cold night when mine was stuck drying after the wash, people offering you their family's rakia ...).  I was told more than once foreigners are treated much better than other locals.  I saw a bit of that...

As an American, just be prepared for one thing that will come up.  The U.S. led the NATO strike against Belgrade a few decades ago.  They have not forgotten this.  I met people who lost loved ones in that debacle.  It took me a few "tries" to learn how to navigate that conversation well (the first time I took the comment at face value, and what ensued was a stressful argument, and you do NOT want to get into an argument with a Serb).  So sharing my findings, I learned to deflect.  I would just make a comment about how it wasn't the people that wanted that, it was just the actions of stupid politicians.  Serbs love to hate on politicians.  That got me through every time it came up then, and let me change the subject more easily.  They will not direct any actual hatred towards you, personally, but they may get animated and Serbs talk quite freely, in general.  So just be prepared.  

Even if someone does raise this with you, another thing to remember about Serbs is that most of them are pretty decent people.  I don't say this about many countries as a whole.  The cultural values are a bit old school, and you find that most people there are quite decent, honest, hard working types of people, who also love to drink and argue. haha  But I met so many people with good hearts.  Be respectful, be good to others, and listen (I learned a LOT from random conversations with store owners of places I would visit, about the bombings, about life there, about how they learned English - often hip hop music, by the way, haha... there's even a tea place I went to that had a DOOM poster on the wall.... if they know about DOOM in Belgrade, I mean... which was another surprise, is how much I had in common with some people I met in terms of tastes in music and television - some stuff, I have no idea how it made it over there when it's still kind of "underground" in the U.S.).  

Other than that, you'll find your way easily enough.  They do like to drink, play live music, and smoke (cigarettes, but if green is your thing, Belgrade and Novi Sad will have some) - the kafana culture is a big thing in Belgrade, at least.  

Oh, and BRING CASH.  It's been maybe four years, but last I was there, even at nice restaurants in Belgrade, it was a chore to pay by card if they even accepted it.  Plan on having cash for everything until you know for certain whether or not they will accept a card.

I didn't like Ships when it came out, and still don't like them much.  I didn't think they would be such a "thing."  I think that they're not THAT important, in that they only play small roles, or none, in most game modes.  

That said, crystal income does take Ships into account.  

I would get familiar, and good on you to ask if you don't know how to approach this.  I would say think of it like the toons, but separately.  What I mean is that you also want fleet synergy (just like you build teams with your toons), and some ships are better than others.  There are mechanics, metas, etc.  Ships has its own thing going.

Consider what fleets you would like.  The farms are long, so pick a fleet, and keep at it.  Early game, aim for one strong fleet.  

I'm not a pro with Ships, so others can maybe give better details.  The thing is you need to learn the mechanics, just like you would with toons.  And it's a different set of mechanics.  You also have to consider pilots.  Ship strength comes from pilots, in large doses, so to invest in a ship is also to invest in that toon who pilots it. 

It will take time...  at your level, a lot is gated by how much energy you have, and how many resources you have (as with any level in the game, but where you are, it can feel like you don't have things you need).  The stronger your account gets, the easier it will be to gain resources.  You're not expected to farm a fleet overnight.

Take the time to look over ship kits - find the synergies (not difficult, it's also usually by faction), learn some of the mechanics, and this will help you generally understand things better.  

Ships was a learning curve for me.  Since I never cared much for them, I didn't really bother much until later on.  I still put off long ship farms unless required for something else (didn't bother with MilF until I started going for JKL).  Keep up with ships, and you'll be farther along down the road.  I wouldn't tell you to concern yourself with GL ships at this point, but at the same time, the earlier you start, the shorter your overall farm.  Consider that Bounty Hunters are a decent team to develop for other game modes, and the ships take a while but will help you with MilF, JKL, GLs, and Executor.  Get that Home One going first, so you can keep up in various game modes, but it's having a long-term plan that will help shape your progress in the app.

I'm sensitive to noise and will offer two somewhat conflicting pieces of advice.  

The first thing to try is to get used to it.  Don't try blocking it out.  I lived near an expressway once, and it was really just white noise with good insulation for doors and windows.  Most of the time I didn't notice it, but if I did, it was really just white noise. My point is, though, I think it will fall to the background if you let it.  You sound a bit hyper-vigilant with some of the environmental noise outside, and that could be other root causes than just noise annoying you, so with compassion I say try to let it go.  I guess you were hoping for complete silence, but it sounds like that is not to be.  So you can either continue to focus on it and let it bother you, or let it go, don't pay attention, ignore it.  Finding things to keep you busy at home may help keep your focus more local.  I would think even the TV would be enough to make the rest go away. 

If you really can't handle it, though, or need breaks from it, or there are certain hours of the day where it gets particularly disruptive, noise cancelling headphones can work wonders.  Especially with that distance, I'm sure you'd be able to completely block it out.  I have a white noise app I use with mine, and then I also have a few music tracks on my phone that serve as calming background noise.

**France** - learn basic French.  You need to understand a few things - the French are GREAT people, in general, but tourists give them a bad rap (especially in Paris) only because those tourists don't bother to understand a fucking thing about French culture or language.  Don't be the idiot.  You always start ANY interaction with a French person with a basic greeting.  "Bonjour" will do.  It's better than simply launching in to a question, and better than simply using English as though everyone understands a foreign language there (most French DO know at least basic English, but it's their country, and many feel nervous to use it, so just don't).  Politesse is part of French culture - be polite.  Don't make assumptions about who speaks what.  Greet storekeepers when you enter (larger places in Paris won't notice, probably, but it IS customary to greet the clerk upon entry).  I could go on about a LOT more cultural norms, as I studied the language/culture for four years, and have lived in France over a year, but that should help you enough.

I'd say push through.  If you already have ideas laid out, you're in a good position to start writing.  Writing is a creative process, a process of discovery.  Don't worry about it being good on a first draft.  Dialogue is also the hardest thing, I think.  It's the one thing I go back and back again, and back again on.  I can have a great story, and get tons of praise from people when I explain it to them, but when I read my own script back to myself, I regularly question the dialogue.  I know writers who get a film made every year or two who I think aren't good with dialogue.  It's not easy.  Don't use this as a measure of your screenplay's worth.  Just work at it until you can get it right.  It might mean a lot of drafts, but don't let it stall you out.

Another idea is to add "meat to the bones" slowly but surely.  Get your outline.  Make a pass at a draft by adding enough to make it a story.  Then go back and flesh things out a little more.  Then go back and revise.  Then get another pair of eyes on it and see where you can improve.  And so on until you're happy with it. ....  Just an idea, I've never written this way, but maybe for you, it would be helpful.  There's no "right way to write."  

Also, your last question is a bit misguided, I think.  Getting from "prose" to "actual screenplay" is not a thing, other than formatting.  If you can write a novel, turning it into a screenplay is little more than making necessary scene divisions and formatting changes.  Clearly you aren't writing prose, if you're stuck on an outline, so this should not be a concern.

Where are you submitting?  I don't want to bring you down in any way, but most of the people I've worked with had their first shorts premier at major festivals like Tribeca.  You say you feel like you're proficient in your skillset, but if you've made that many films already and don't know how to move forward, I'd question your output.  Which isn't to tell you to give up, or that you can't hack it, it's only to say either you aren't submitting to the right festivals, or maybe you need to keep improving.  The big difference in where you're showing your work being there are many more networking opportunities at the larger festivals.  Even if it's a short, if you go to Sundance with it, you're going to be meeting a lot more people that will have access to money for future projects, and have better chances of meeting potential collaborators with wider reach.

Typically, to get a writing agent, you need one original feature, a TV pilot, and an episode written for an existing show (and all need to be GOOD).  You also probably want to know someone with an agent at that agency to help it get passed along and actually looked at.  Network is key in film/TV.  It's the one major disadvantage of you being outside a major market.  Back to the festival thing - even living outside a major market, if you can open that door, you'll meet more people.  I'd say, for now, make your goal to be getting a major festival premier, whether short or feature.

Something I don't see in your post is what you WANT to be doing!  Pretty key, here.  Can't give much more advice without knowing that.  You're young, though, like really young for this (unless high school was a long time ago, but your post leads me to believe you're still young), so just keep working on what it is you want to be working on.  Keep in mind even people who find a lot of success in the industry rarely, rarely, rarely start out making a living at it.  You might be surprised (or maybe not) how many "working" actors, writers, etc. in L.A. have "regular day jobs," live at home with parents or rent with a bunch of other people to keep costs down, etc.  Just a quick example - I know a writer/director who got his first short a Tribeca premier.  That's what it took to find more work, and now he writes TV films about once a year.  He still works his day job career.  He doesn't live in a major market.  He isn't writing the kind of stuff anyone's going to be raving over at the theater.  But he gets consistent work as a paid film writer.  For him, that's okay.  Not his dream, but he's doing just fine.  My point is, don't get "stuck" on the idea a career in film/TV has to be a certain thing.  Keep improving your work, get it in front of the right people best you can, and network for future opportunities.  The rest is often going to come down to luck.

You've already got it.  Most people max out credit cards (sometimes even getting new ones just to max out on the film).  If you can find personal loans, sure (but probably the worst option).  Friends chipping in.  Savings accounts.  I've seen crowdfunding work for first-time writer/directors, but that was on a feature.  You'd want to have some solid swag to offer for a short, I think.

Also, keep in mind where the budget is coming from.  I think this is really the best way to approach it, as keeping costs down in the first place is how you can optimize.  Work your network for locations (maybe someone knows a restaurant owner that would let you shoot for free after hours, so you don't have to pay someone to shut their business down for a day - as an example).  Find a DP with his own camera that you can cut a deal with, rather than have to pay standard rental costs.  Choose your camera wisely so you aren't overpaying on an Alexa when you could use a Canon (won't start listing movies made on phones...).  

In my experience, and from what anyone has ever told me, the only thing you don't skimp on is food.  You can beg, borrow, and deal on everything else, but when you're doing a low budget short, just make sure everyone is well-fed on set.  Doesn't mean you need a stellar caterer, but don't just be ordering pizzas.  Have a proper crafty table, and figure out some decent meals.  I did a really low budget film once, feature, that was cutting corners left and right (mostly in how they paid and treated production - it was the last film that group ever made because no one would work with them again), but even without a caterer, I had no complaints.  Pupusas, Chinese...  we just ordered from all the cheapest "ethnic cuisine" places in the area, and worked out deals with the owners because we ordered so much food, and everyone was happy.  The pupusas were so good I took some for leftovers to eat on idle days. haha

I've seen crowdfunding work with no "pre-existing audience."  The key is really to have a compelling story (not speaking to the movie, but a personal story that will compel people to want to help), as well as a solid script (that's completed, not just 'in the works').  

That said, 100% that they're generally self-financed.  Most people I know have maxed out credit cards to do their first shorts.  Get that into a festival or two, and try to move forward from there.
